extracted.intended_audience: teachers, curriculum planners, and students of education
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for teaching and organizing history, geography, nature study, and science in school curricula so that subject matter enriches experience, fosters curiosity, and connects to present social life and practical activities. Emphasizes methods (psychological vs logical), integration of subjects, and avoiding fragmentary or ritualistic instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information must be informing (not mere accumulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional material should be 'informing'—insight gained fuses with what is told, enabling individual experience to take up and hold the group's results; there is no fixed saturation point for assimilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance stresses that mere amassing of information apart from immediate interests makes the mind 'wooden' and reduces elasticity. Good instruction increases receptiveness and curiosity; new receptiveness follows information gained. Anti-pattern: piling up facts that do not enlarge the meaning of ordinary experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects should furnish background and outlook
rubrics_metrics.description: History and geography should supply subject matter that gives background, outlook, and intellectual perspective so ordinary actions gain significant content in their time and space connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching should enable pupils to 'place our own doings in their time and space connections' so daily experiences 'gain enduring substance.' If taught otherwise, subjects become alien lists rather than contextualizing resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching subject-matter as ready-made isolated studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present geography, history, or nature-study as ready-made stores of remote facts studied simply because pupils are sent to school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: dividing activity into two separate worlds (school facts vs ordinary life), creating unassimilated loads of information, making mind 'wooden.' Remedy: integrate facts with pupils' immediate activities and interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link studies to immediate activity to animate learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter must be made real by entering into immediate activity so ordinary experience is enlarged in meaning by its connections with studied material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: to 'learn geography' is to gain power to perceive spatial connections; to 'learn history' is to recognize human connections. If not linked, studies remain inert; instruction must render consequences and connections perceptible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate curiosity by rewarding reaching-out of experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiosity is intrinsic to moving, changing experiences and tends to make conditions perceptible; educators must supply environments that reward and sustain this reaching out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning environments so activities lead students to seek additional information rather than passively receive it. Anti-pattern: environments that check activity so only direct, tangible outcomes accrue.

rubrics_metrics.name: History and geography are complementary and unified
rubrics_metrics.description: Geography emphasizes the physical side and history the social, but both are phases of the same whole: the associated life of men which occurs in nature as its medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should emphasize the interdependence of man and nature; ignoring this makes history a listing of dates or literary phantasy and geography a rag-bag of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach geography with human bearings, not as fragmentary facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic data must be tied to the residence, pursuits, successes, and failures of men so they have reason for inclusion; local geography should be a starting point for understanding the larger world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting disconnected items (height of a mountain, course of a river) without human context. Use imagination and travel/adventure stimulus; treat local facts as leads into broader political, economic, and natural connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center specialized geographical branches on humane/cultural aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialties (mathematical, physiographic, political, commercial geography) should be adjusted by keeping the educational center of gravity in the cultural or humane aspects of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material is relevant only insofar as it helps appreciate human activities and relations. Specializations are for specialists; for general education emphasize interactions that concern social life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include nature study as integral to earth/geography study
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature study should be treated as a study of nature-as-whole, not as isolated fragments (parts of a flower apart from plant and soil), so phenomena fall into natural relations with human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: scrappy subject matter leading to deadness and resort to animism or sentimental personification. Remedy: present plants, animals, and phenomena in their contexts (soil, air, light, human uses).

rubrics_metrics.name: History must be connected to present social life
rubrics_metrics.description: The past must be taught as the history of the present: study of past events should illuminate present conditions and begin from present situations with their problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genetic method (trace processes of making) to render complex present conditions comprehensible. Anti-pattern: treating past as unrelated, leading to 'Let the dead bury their dead' attitude or inert memorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use biographical method with social context
rubrics_metrics.description: Biographies of great men condense complex events into vivid pictures, but must not exaggerate individual deeds without reference to the social situations they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: isolating heroes from conditions (sugar coating). Good use links life-stories to the social forces and circumstances they respond to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use study of primitive life as simplified model for present problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive conditions can reduce present complex social relationships to their simplest form and thus help understand the genesis of present institutions and problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct use reveals fundamental problems of subsistence, shelter, protection, and invention; misuse treats primitive life as sensational 'savagery' devoid of social aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include industrial/economic history to illuminate common life
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial history reveals the successive inventions and adaptations by which man has mastered nature and thereby shows the activities and values of the common man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This branch is more democratic and liberalizing than political/military history and gives direct insight into occupations, production, distribution, and social progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach intellectual history to show role of ideas and invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize scientific discoverers, inventors, artists, and poets—those whose methods and creations expanded human capacity and accessibility of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter the false impression that human intellect is static; show how intellectual methods and inventions drove progress and shaped historical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: History's moral value is in cultivating socialized intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: History should foster intelligent insight into present social forms, enabling moral development beyond mere anecdotal moralizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using history merely as a reservoir of moral anecdotes or to inculcate special moral lessons; instead use it to analyze the warp and woof of present social fabric for permanent ethical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish logical (expert) and psychological (learner) approaches to science
rubrics_metrics.description: Science in perfected logical form is the expert's organization of knowledge; the psychological/chronological method begins with the learner's experience and develops scientific treatment from that starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not start novices with technical deductive forms and definitions; although seeming faster, this isolates science from meaningful experience. The psychological method secures understanding and lasting interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting science as symbols or technical vocabulary alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing laws, definitions, and technical concepts at the outset makes pupils learn a 'science' of symbols rather than the scientific way of treating familiar material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: pupils acquire a peculiar vocabulary without tracing connections to objects and operations. Good practice grounds terms in problems and activities where they function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory exercises must connect to real problems and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact with things and laboratory manipulation are indispensable but do not constitute scientific method by themselves if disassociated from ordinary-life materials and problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ritualistic lab practices that emphasize technical manipulation for its own sake. Labs should be tied to problems belonging to subject matter and to pupils' experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach scientific terminology as functional tools, not names
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific signs and symbols denote elements of a cognitive system and their significance is learned by use; knowing names is not knowing the function they perform in the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should show what concepts accomplish in the system (e.g., how a formula functions in problem solving), analogous to knowing parts of a machine by their uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use science education to modify ends and foster novel purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Education in science should cultivate intelligence that can form new purposes and modify habitual aims, not merely provide improved means for preexisting desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science should be taught so it shapes imagination and feeling toward progressive ends (belief in the possibility of directing human affairs), avoiding mere technical mastery that leaves ends unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enculturate empirical-rational habits through science
rubrics_metrics.description: Science education should foster emancipation from 'rule of thumb' and crude empirical attitudes, instilling habits of testing, reflection, and rational control of means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize method: observation, reflection, testing, revising beliefs. The goal is an intelligence that looks to the future and believes in human capacity to direct and improve social conditions.
